summary: Meridiano Lunar helps people compare landing sites and dates near the Moon’s south pole. The interactive explorer shows how sunlight and a direct line of sight to Earth change as users switch sites or move through time. Our demonstration uses NASA terrain data and JPL ephemerides to compare three sites for a four-day mission. It illustrates how an AI agent could explain the best match for a mission’s requirements and suggest alternatives when dates or priorities change.
details:
Meridiano Lunar addresses the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. Its web prototype lets users select a region and date on a south pole map, move through hours of the day, and compare two scenarios for sunlight and direct Earth visibility. The prototype uses illustrative visibility values to demonstrate the interaction.

The slide demonstration uses NASA LRO/LOLA terrain and JPL Horizons ephemerides to estimate when the Sun and Earth are above the local terrain horizon. For a mission from January 12 through 15, 2030, it compares three sites by total simultaneous visibility, the longest continuous window, and estimated terrain slope. Peak Near Shackleton has both the Sun and Earth in view throughout the four-day window in this calculation. If the dates can move, Connecting Ridge has a comparable window from January 4 through 7.

The AI recommendation workflow shown in the slides takes a mission’s dates and requirements, ranks the candidate sites by those criteria, and explains the alternatives in terms of the underlying calculations. The project aims to make these trade-offs easier to inspect for mission teams, educators, and learners. The explorer uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, and the calculations for the slide demonstration were prepared with Python, NumPy, and Rasterio.
